answer.sourceLine: This is Analects 1.1 — the opening sentence of the entire book, 學而時習之，不亦說乎, recorded as the words of “the Master” by Confucius’s disciples. The English you see quoted, however, is not ancient: it matches A. Charles Muller’s translation ↗, which he dates to the summer of 1990.

source.excerpt:
子曰：「學而時習之，不亦說乎？有朋自遠方來，不亦樂乎？人不知而不慍，不亦君子乎？」

James Legge’s English (The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 — wording as in the revised edition, which is the text Project Gutenberg and ctext print): “The Master said, ‘Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters? Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?’”
trail: The line is not a floating aphorism — it is Analects 1.1, the very first passage of the book, and Book 1’s Chinese title 學而 is simply its opening two characters. The Chinese Text Project ↗ prints the original 子曰：「學而時習之，不亦說乎？…」 beside James Legge’s English.

The English wording quoted today matches A. Charles Muller’s translation of the Analects ↗, whose own page records the translation as first made in the summer of 1990 and last revised on 1 December 2021.

The public-domain English reads very differently. Legge’s version — “Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? ↗” — appears in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1, listed on Wikisource ↗ as “Vol. I (1861 & 1893)”.

Confucius left no book of his own. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy ↗ reports the traditional account — Ban Gu’s, second century CE — that the Analects was compiled by first- and second-generation disciples, while noting that recent scholarship disputes its status as the oldest stratum, since writers only took an acute interest in the text in the late second and first centuries BCE.
source.excerptNote: The excerpt deliberately shows the public-domain text — the Chinese original and Legge’s English. It is his revised wording, the version Project Gutenberg and ctext carry; his 1861 first edition renders the second clause “Is it not pleasant to have friends coming from distant quarters?”, and only the first clause is identical in both editions. The wording people actually share, “Isn’t it a pleasure to study and practice what you have learned?”, is A. Charles Muller’s translation of that same first clause.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: Confucius, who wrote nothing
author.metaLine: c. 551 – c. 479 BCE · Chinese philosopher and teacher of the Spring and Autumn period, from the state of Lu
author.bio: Confucius was a teacher and sometime official from the state of Lu, in what is now Qufu, Shandong, traditionally dated to c. 551 – c. 479 BCE and long regarded as the paragon of Chinese sages. He wrote no book: his teachings survive as sayings recorded by his students and compiled into the Analects, largely during the Warring States period, with the text reaching its final form in the mid-Han dynasty. That gap is why modern scholars are careful about attributing any specific sentence to the man himself — and why every English “Confucius quote” is at minimum a translator’s reading of a disciple’s note.

misattribution.heading: Nobody stole this one — but the English has no name on it
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare cases where the famous name is the right one. The sentence really does open Confucius’s book. What goes missing every time it is shared is who wrote the English.

items.why: “Isn’t it a pleasure to study and practice what you have learned?” is a modern rendering of 學而時習之，不亦說乎, and it matches the wording in Muller’s Analects translation ↗, which he dates to the summer of 1990. Confucius spoke classical Chinese; the memorable English sentence is a named living-memory translator’s work.

items.scope: The source line on quote sites
items.who: “The Analects, Chapter I” with no translator
items.why: AZQuotes ↗ gives the source as “The Analects. Book by Confucius (Chapter I)” and names no translator at all — so a reader has no way to tell a 1990 English sentence from an ancient one.

Only the third clause differs. Both AZQuotes and Wikiquote ↗ end “isn’t he a sage?”, while Muller’s current page ends “am I not a noble man?” (his 2010 revision read “am I not a Gentleman?”). The first two clauses are word-for-word Muller — including “Isn’t it also great when friends visit from distant places?”. Wikiquote’s Chapter I header credits its English to Legge’s 1861 translation, yet Legge’s rendering of this line reads nothing like the one printed there.

He wrote none of it. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy ↗ reports the traditional account — Ban Gu’s, second century CE — that the Analects was compiled by first- and second-generation disciples, while noting that recent scholarship disputes its standing as the oldest stratum; Wikipedia’s article on the text ↗ notes that large portions were composed during the Warring States period (475–221 BC), with the work reaching final form in the mid-Han dynasty.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is genuinely Confucius’s — it opens the Analects at 1.1 ↗. The English sentence everyone shares belongs to a named modern translator.

context.heading: Why the first line of the Analects is the first line
lead: The Analects opens with a three-part sketch of a life worth living, and this is its first move: learning is a pleasure when it is actually used. The passage is foundational enough that Book 1 takes its Chinese title, 學而, straight from the sentence’s opening two characters — the book is literally named after this line.

It is also a clean demonstration of how much work a translator does. In 1861 James Legge turned the clause into “Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?” Around 1990 A. Charles Muller turned the same clause into “Isn’t it a pleasure to study and practice what you have learned?” Only one of those went viral — and it is the one still under copyright.
detailsBody: Wikiquote lists this rendering in its Analects Chapter I section directly beneath the Chinese original, and its section header attributes the English to Legge’s 1861 translation — but Legge’s rendering of this line reads nothing like the one printed, so the sentence is not merely uncredited, it is credited to the wrong translator.
Aggregators reproduce the sentence as though it were the ancient text itself. AZQuotes cites “The Analects. Book by Confucius (Chapter I)” and stops there, naming no translator and no edition.

If you need a version you can reprint freely, use Legge. The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 is listed on Wikisource as “Vol. I (1861 & 1893)”, is public domain in the United States, and the full text is at Project Gutenberg.
context.pull: The thought is Confucius’s. The sentence is A. Charles Muller’s.
